author.name: Mikhail Bulgakov
author.biography: Bulgakov was born in Kiev and trained as a doctor before turning to writing in Moscow in the 1920s, where his plays made him famous and then made him a target. By the end of the decade his work was banned from the stage and from print. He worked on this novel for the last twelve years of his life, burning one draft and rewriting the rest, with little hope of seeing it published. It appeared more than a quarter of a century after his death.

hook.text: What would the devil find if he came to Moscow to see how people live?

paragraphs: A foreign professor of black magic arrives in Moscow with three strange companions and spends a few spring days among its editors, poets, theater managers and housing officials. Wherever he goes, people's greed, vanity and fear come out into the open, often in ways that are extremely funny.

Woven through this comedy is a second story, told in quite another voice: the day on which Pontius Pilate questions a wandering philosopher in Yershalaim and has to decide what to do with him. It is the work of a writer known only as the master, whose novel cost him everything, and of the woman who refuses to give him up.

Bulgakov lets the two stories comment on each other. Pilate's choice and its consequences cast a long shadow over a city where people inform on neighbors and critics attack books they know to be good. The novel is severe about cowardice and generous toward almost everyone in it.
Read it for the jokes and for the solemn chapters alike. What does a person owe to the truth when telling it is dangerous, and what can love or mercy do for those who failed?

orientation.text: Two stories alternate: Moscow in the 1930s, and Yershalaim on the day of Pilate's judgment. Many people have several names: Koroviev is also Fagot, and Ivan Nikolayevich writes as Bezdomny.
